cards.title: Circuit noise tolerance beyond the formula threshold
cards.formal:
Put \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\). For \(0\le p<1/2\), let \(\mathcal C_p(n)\) be the finite noisy circuits defined below. Define reliable computation at noise \(p\) by \[\operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff \exists\delta\in(0,1/2]\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}\ \exists C\in\mathcal C_p(n)\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\Pr[C(x)=f(x)]\ge1/2+\delta.\] Does there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2-\beta)\) such that
\[\operatorname{Reliable}(\beta+\varepsilon)?\]
The positive increase in noise tolerance is fixed independently of the Boolean function and its input length. Any such positive constant qualifies.
cards.definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with labeled input sources \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), noiseless constant sources \(0,1\), and one designated output wire. A computational gate has one or two ordered input wires and an arbitrary fixed Boolean truth table on those bits. Wires may connect a source or an earlier gate to any number of later gates; both inputs of a gate may come from the same predecessor. There are no other gates, external coins, auxiliary inputs, or oracle operations. A gate-free output is allowed to read one source directly.

For every computational gate \(v\), independently sample \(Z_v\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr[Z_v=1]=p\). Evaluate the DAG in topological order. If the gate truth table applied to its received bits gives \(b\), its actual value is \(b\mathbin{\oplus}Z_v\), where \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. Every outgoing wire carries this same actual value. All gate failures are mutually independent and independent of the input; wire values sharing a predecessor need not be independent. Input sources and wires are perfect. All computational gates, including NOT and any output gate, have exactly the same flip probability \(p\); no noiseless output decoder is supplied.

The probability in the target is only over this finite product of gate-failure distributions, for a fixed input \(x\). The circuit and its wiring and truth tables may depend on the real parameter \(p\), the integer \(n\), and the entire function \(f\), but not on the actual input \(x\) or realized failures. The advantage \(\delta\) may depend on \(p\), but is chosen before \(n\) and \(f\). Circuit size, depth and construction time are unrestricted, and no uniform algorithm constructing the circuits is required. A formula is the special case where every computational gate has at most one outgoing wire; an input variable can still occur on multiple leaves.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that reliable computation is possible at some noise level strictly above \(\beta\), or a proof that it is impossible at every \(p\in(\beta,1/2)\), in the specified independent gate-flip model. No particular positive increase in noise tolerance is prescribed. At a fixed noise level, the same positive correctness advantage must work for all input lengths and all Boolean functions. Reliability only at \(p=\beta\) does not answer this strict-crossing question. A negative answer must exclude all finite circuit sizes, not just one construction. Restricted gate bases, noiseless decoders and different error models do not establish the full claim. The answer is a proposition, without a numerical \(1/100\) tolerance.
cards.why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.

importance.reason: A sharp reliability boundary for general classical computation, separating the effects of gate errors from circuit size and design effort.

context_blocks.text: The task concerns whether arbitrary computation remains possible at all under local errors, even when unlimited redundancy is permitted. The target keeps a positive correctness margin independent of the function and its number of inputs. It is not a circuit-size overhead problem or an average over randomly chosen inputs.

Unger’s theorem gives the sharp formula boundary \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\), including failure of universal reliable computation at equality, and explicitly conjectures the extension to circuits. Formulas cannot reuse an intermediate noisy gate value; circuits can, so independent gate failures do not make the received signals independent. The positive formula result below \(\beta\) also provides circuits.

The later formulation of reliable computation in Definition 2.1 of Shutty, Wootters and Hayden uses one advantage for all Boolean functions, as here. Their survey distinguishes the symmetric two-input formula threshold from the known general-circuit upper bound \(1/2-1/(2\sqrt{2})\). Their main asymmetric model permits gate-dependent errors, including noiseless XOR, and its proposed circuit extension is conditional. Those statements do not settle the identical-noise circuit claim.

The July 2025 essay revisits established circuit-noise bounds and discusses majority gates of higher arity. Its stated scope does not supply the missing exact threshold for arbitrary two-input circuits.

The original circuit conjecture also rules out reliable computation exactly at \(p=\beta\). The user's 17 September 2026 choice focuses this card on a strictly positive improvement above the formula threshold. The new target separates that strict crossing from the endpoint question; it is not claimed equivalent to the original boundary-inclusive conjecture.

cards.title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm \(A\), and a constant \(C>0\) such that \(A\) properly colors every simple \(n\)-vertex graph with a supplied valid maximum-degree bound \(\Delta\ge2\), using colors in \(\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}\), within
\[C\bigl(\Delta^{1/2-\varepsilon}+\log^* n\bigr)\]
synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct \(O(\log n)\)-bit identifiers and know \(n\) and \(\Delta\). Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The same \(\varepsilon,A,C\) must work for every admissible \(n,\Delta\), graph and identifier assignment.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm and some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) meeting the stated uniform round bound, or of the logical negation of this existence statement. The improvement may be arbitrarily small but must be one positive constant independent of both \(n\) and \(\Delta\). A negative answer must rule out every positive constant exponent saving in the stated model. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent \(1/2\), or allowing the saving to tend to zero with input size, does not meet the target. There is no prescribed minimum saving and no numerical \(1/100\) answer tolerance for this proposition.
cards.why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
cards.definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target. The exponent saving is chosen before the graph parameters; it is not an accuracy input that must be handled uniformly by a family of algorithms.

progress.text: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette.
Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence.

The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

Suomela's list gives the concrete exponent \(0.499\) as one example of crossing the square-root degree barrier. Following the user's 17 September 2026 formulation choice, this card asks for any fixed exponent \(1/2-\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon>0\), rather than the particular saving \(0.001\). This broadens the original fixed-threshold question: a smaller positive saving also qualifies. The palette, determinism and additive \(\log^* n\) term remain part of the model.

cards.title: Sub-base-two exact shortest common superstring
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform deterministic classical word-RAM algorithm \(A\), a constant \(K>0\), and integers \(d\ge2\) and \(a\ge1\) such that, for every list of \(n\ge0\) explicitly given finite strings over any finite alphabet, \(A\) outputs a shortest common superstring within
\[K(2-\varepsilon)^n(L+1)^a\]
machine steps? Here \(L\) is the total binary input length, and words have \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil)\) bits. All constants, including the positive base improvement \(\varepsilon\), are fixed independently of the number, lengths and alphabet of the input strings.
cards.why: The problem asks whether the classical exponential cost of ordering many overlapping strings can be reduced by a fixed factor in the exponent. It is a central exact-algorithm question for sequence assembly and helps distinguish the complexity of string overlap from more general ordering problems.
cards.status_note: Source-open in Kulikov’s 2013 seminar question and the 2019 unrestricted exact-algorithms discussion. A bounded check through 2026-09-16 found no verified resolution of the deterministic classical exact-algorithms questions reviewed there. Bounded-string-length, quantum and approximation results have different assumptions or guarantees.

cards.definitions:
The alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}\), where \(\sigma\ge1\) is supplied with the input and \(\sigma\le\max\{1,\sum_i|s_i|\}\). This is a representation convention: arbitrary finite input alphabets can be relabeled by consecutive integers without changing the number of strings, containment, or optimum output length. A string is an explicitly listed finite sequence of alphabet symbols. A string \(s\) is a substring of \(z\) if \(z=u s v\) for finite strings \(u,v\); its occurrence must be contiguous. A common superstring of \(s_1,\ldots,s_n\) contains every \(s_i\) as a substring. It is shortest if no common superstring has fewer symbols. The output must be an actual shortest superstring, not just a superstring of approximately optimal length. Multiple optimum outputs are allowed. For \(n=0\), the optimum is the empty string.

For definiteness, encode a nonnegative integer \(z\) by \(1^b0\,\operatorname{bin}(z)\), where \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\), other binary numerals have no leading zeroes, and \(b\) is the numeral length. The input consists of these codes for \(\sigma,n\), followed, for each string in order, by a code for its length and then its symbols in \(h=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2\sigma\rceil\}\) bits each. Every encoded symbol must be less than \(\sigma\). The concatenation has \(L\) bits, with no trailing data. The output uses the same length-and-symbol convention. The parameter \(n\) is the number of strings in this supplied list, before any algorithmic preprocessing; it is not the total number of symbols or the maximum string length. Empty strings, duplicates and strings contained in others are permitted. There is no bound on the maximum string length in terms of \(n\), no fixed-alphabet restriction, and no promise on pairwise overlaps.

The RAM receives \(n,L\) in designated input registers in addition to the encoded input. It has a fixed finite program, a constant number of registers and random-access words indexed by \(w\)-bit addresses. Its word operations are copying, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), bitwise Boolean operations, shifts with discarded overflow, unsigned comparison and conditional branching. A shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Reading or writing one addressed memory word, reading an input word or writing an output word costs one step, as does each arithmetic or control instruction. Input bits are packed into words and padded with zeroes beyond the known input length \(L\); padding is not part of the input. Words initially outside the input and fixed initialization are zero. Values exceeding one word must be represented by multiple words with all operations charged. There is no unbounded unit-cost arithmetic, nonuniform advice, oracle, randomness or quantum operation. The program and constants \(K,d,a\) do not depend on \(n,L,\sigma\) or the input strings. All parsing, preprocessing, memory accesses and output writing count. No separate polynomial-space requirement is imposed. The bound is worst-case for every valid input.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such an algorithm and some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), including exact optimality of every output and the stated uniform worst-case resource bound, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation. Any positive constant improvement below base two qualifies; there is no required saving of \(0.01\) and no numerical acceptance tolerance. A negative answer must exclude every fixed base below two in the specified machine model. A result only for a fixed maximum input-string length, a quantum algorithm, a polynomial-time approximation, or a saving that vanishes with input size does not settle this target. A conditional lower bound alone does not establish unconditional nonexistence.

context_blocks.text: The 2013 seminar report gives the concrete target \(O^*(1.99^n)\), where \(n\) counts input strings. The present card follows the user's 17 September 2026 choice to accept any fixed base below two. It retains the deterministic classical word-RAM interpretation previously selected for this card; the short original source does not itself specify randomization or a detailed machine. Bounded-length strings and a reduction from Traveling Salesman are separate questions in that report.

The known baseline is \(O^*(2^n)\), with the star suppressing a fixed polynomial in total input length. The 2013 report states that polynomial space is possible at this baseline; it does not require polynomial space of the requested faster algorithm.

Golovnev, Kulikov and Mihajlin give a randomized algorithm for strings of length at most a fixed \(r\), with time \(O^*(2^{(1-1/(2r^2+1))n})\). Its improvement depends on the length bound, which is absent from the main question.

The 2019 paper asks for an exact classical \(O^*((2-\varepsilon)^n)\) algorithm on unrestricted strings for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). This is the barrier formulation now adopted: the improvement is independent of all input sizes, but no particular positive amount is prescribed.

Khadiev and Bosch Machado report a bounded-error quantum \(O^*(1.728^n)\) bound. Their Section 2.1 formulates equal-length input strings, and Section 2.2 defines quantum query cost as running time. This does not establish the unrestricted classical bound with all machine work charged.

An August 2026 preprint reports a \(7/3\)-approximation for general shortest common superstring and a factor \(3\) guarantee for the greedy algorithm. These concern approximation quality, not the exact exponential-time target.

cards.title: Breaking two for metric k-Median
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\), and integers \(K,b\ge1\) such that, for every valid metric k-Median input \(I\) of bit length \(L\), every execution of \(A\) finishes within \(KL^b\) bit steps and returns a nonempty set \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|\le k\), while
\[\Pr[\operatorname{cost}(S)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)]\ge2/3?\]
The input, cost and computation model are specified below. The same positive \(\varepsilon\), program and polynomial constants must work for every input, facility budget, metric size and distance precision. No unproved complexity assumption is included.
cards.definitions:
An input is \(I=(v,C,F,k,d)\), with \(v\ge1\), \(V=[v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\), nonempty \(C,F\subseteq V\), \(C\cup F=V\), and an integer \(1\le k\le|F|\). The sets may overlap. The full table \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) is promised to be a metric: \(d(x,y)=d(y,x)\), \(d(x,y)=0\) if and only if \(x=y\), and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all points. There are no weights or capacities: each client in \(C\) has unit demand, and facilities must be chosen from the supplied \(F\).

For a nonempty \(S\subseteq F\), let \[\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{c\in C}\min_{s\in S}d(c,s),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}=\min_{S\subseteq F,\ 1\le|S|\le k}\operatorname{cost}(S).\] Both minima are over finite nonempty sets. The output need only specify the selected facilities; no assignment or optimality certificate is required. Feasibility is mandatory even on random executions where the approximation inequality fails. No extra facilities are allowed in such executions or merely on average. Zero optimum is included: in that case the successful executions must have exactly zero cost. In a metric this case occurs precisely when \(C\subseteq F\) and \(|C|\le k\); a quotient by the optimum is never used in the definition.

Fix a concrete binary encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(t\), write \(u(t)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\), where \(\operatorname{bin}\) has no leading zeros and \(a\) is its length. The input concatenates \(u(v)\), \(u(k)\), the two \(v\)-bit membership masks for \(C,F\), and the \(v^2\) rational entries in row-major order. An entry is a reduced pair \(p/q\) with integers \(p\ge0,q\ge1\), encoded by \(u(p)u(q)\); zero uses \(p=0,q=1\). The total length of this entire string is \(L\). A facility set is output as a \(v\)-bit membership mask. No bound on numerators or denominators is assumed beyond their finite encoding.

The model is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, a read-only input tape, initially blank work and output tapes, and ordinary charged tape transitions. A random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. Running time counts every transition, including preprocessing, arithmetic, random-bit generation and output; the stated polynomial bound holds on every random execution. There is no advice depending on input length, oracle, quantum operation or unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic. Behavior on strings outside the input promise is irrelevant. Success probability is over the random bits for each fixed input, not over an input distribution, and no single choice of coins must work for all inputs.

The positive improvement is fixed before the input and is not an input parameter. The program and its time polynomial may depend on that fixed improvement, but cannot vary with the input size, facility budget or distance precision. There is no extra geometric or structural promise.

For background notation, let \(\mathcal R\) be the factors \(r\ge1\) achievable by one uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm per factor with the same all-executions feasibility and per-input \(2/3\) success convention. Put \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}=\inf\mathcal R\). Known constant-factor algorithms make this set nonempty. The current target asks whether \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}<2\), not for a numerical determination of the infimum or its attainment.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) meeting all stated guarantees, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation. Any positive constant improvement below factor two qualifies; there is no prescribed \(1/100\) improvement or numerical answer tolerance. Every execution must obey the polynomial bit-time bound and the facility budget, and each fixed input must satisfy the approximation inequality with probability at least \(2/3\). A negative answer must rule out every positive constant saving for the allowed randomized algorithms. An expected-only facility budget, a fixed-parameter running time in \(k\), restricted metrics, or a result only about an LP integrality gap does not settle the target. A hardness conclusion under an unproved complexity assumption remains conditional.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for a tight approximation result. The current card selects the strict-below-two question under the user's 17 September 2026 barrier rule. The standard LP has gap approaching two, while the established true-budget algorithms approach two from above. This makes a fixed improvement below two a concrete barrier question without assuming that two is the optimal ratio for unrestricted algorithms.

Metric k-Median chooses service locations and minimizes the sum of client travel distances. It also models selecting representatives for clustering. Clients and candidate facilities may be different sets, and the metric need not have Euclidean coordinates. The unresolved ratio measures how much optimization quality is lost when an arbitrary metric instance must be processed in polynomial time.

The known unconditional bounds give \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{med}}\le2\). The upper endpoint follows from the \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\); it does not assert a factor-two algorithm. Under \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), the coverage hardness below gives \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}\ge1+2/e\approx1.73576\). These are different kinds of bounds. In particular, \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) would imply \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}=1\).

Feige’s Theorem 5.3 gives an NP-hard coverage gap: all elements can be covered by \(k\) sets, or every such collection covers at most a \(1-1/e+\eta\) fraction, for any fixed \(\eta>0\). The associated client–facility metric uses separate copies of elements and sets, with cross distances one for incidence and three otherwise, and distance two between distinct points on the same side. Covering a fraction \(p\) corresponds to cost \((3-2p)|U|\), where \(U\) is the universe. Thus the gap becomes \(1\) versus \(1+2/e-2\eta\) per client.

This gap also explains the randomized assumption. A returned feasible solution of sufficiently small cost certifies the positive side; on a negative instance no such solution exists. Consequently a bounded-error algorithm beating the threshold would put the underlying NP-hard decision problem in \(\mathrm{RP}\), the class with polynomial time, one-sided error and no false acceptance. The exclusion for this card is therefore conditional on \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), rather than justified by \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 Theorem 10 instead derives the classical k-Median lower bound from a Set Cover approximation barrier. The historical complexity assumption stated there is \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{DTIME}(n^{O(\log\log n)})\). Feige’s ordinary NP-hardness theorem for Max k-Cover and its metric gap distinguish the stronger coverage-based conclusion from the assumption in that earlier Set Cover argument.

Theorem 1.1 of the STOC 2025 paper, retained in its May 2026 full revision, gives a randomized polynomial-time \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with a feasible facility budget. The separate Theorem 1.2 allows extra centers, but this is not the budget of the final theorem. Lemma 1.4 relates bounded integer distances to general distances, so the result is not confined to a fixed distance precision.

Byrka and coauthors’ April 2026 paper supplies another \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for metric k-Median, in Corollary 1.2. Its intermediate guarantee opens \(k\) facilities only in expectation; the final approximation restores the facility budget with an \(\varepsilon\) loss. This distinction matters: an expected budget permits some outcomes with too many facilities and does not meet the card’s all-executions feasibility requirement. The new result does not narrow the interval between the known conditional lower endpoint and two.

The standard linear relaxation has fractional openings \(0\le y_s\le1\), assignments \(0\le x_{c,s}\le y_s\), \(\sum_s x_{c,s}=1\) for every client, and \(\sum_s y_s\le k\), minimizing \(\sum_{c,s}d(c,s)x_{c,s}\). Its integrality gap approaches two. For a unit-edge star with \(q\ge3\) leaves, all vertices as facilities, leaves as clients and \(k=q-1\), the integral optimum is two. A feasible fractional solution has center opening \(1/(q-1)\), each leaf opening \((q-2)/(q-1)\), and each client assigned to its own leaf and the center in those proportions. Its cost is \(q/(q-1)\), yielding a gap at least \(2(q-1)/q\). This is a barrier for that relaxation, not an unconditional computational lower bound against the true integral optimum.

Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 Theorem 1 attains \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in time \(f(k,\varepsilon)n^{O(1)}\). That fixed-parameter guarantee allows a dependence on \(k\) which need not be polynomial. Here \(k\) is part of the unrestricted input, so the parameterized result does not establish the corresponding polynomial-time factor.
The March 2026 low-dimensional Euclidean work improves approximation-scheme running times by using geometric structure. Its guarantees do not apply to arbitrary metric tables.

The July 2026 spectral dual-fitting preprint improves k-Means guarantees in Euclidean and general metrics. That objective sums squared distances, which changes both approximation and hardness constants; the paper does not give a smaller general k-Median ratio.

A polynomial-time factor \(2-\varepsilon\), for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), would cross the selected barrier for general metric clustering. Feasibility, probability and runtime must refer to the same input model. A restricted metric theorem, an LP gap or an expected-budget guarantee addresses a different question.

cards.title: Breaking two for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid instance \(I\) of the scheduling problem defined below, \(A\) outputs a feasible schedule \(S_A(I)\) within \(K(L(I)+2)^d\) bit steps and
\[C_{\max}(S_A(I))\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\]
Here \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length. The same positive \(\varepsilon\), program and polynomial bound must work for every job count, machine count and remaining input parameter. The complete instance is supplied before scheduling begins. No unproved complexity assumption is included in this existence question.
cards.definitions:
An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same fixed-factor approximation-existence question.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside \(\mathcal I\). The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

cards.title: Breaking two for precedence-constrained makespan
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid instance \(I\) of the scheduling problem defined below, \(A\) outputs a feasible schedule \(S_A(I)\) within \(K(L(I)+1)^d\) bit steps and
\[C_{\max}(S_A(I))\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\]
Here \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length. The same positive \(\varepsilon\), program and polynomial bound must work for every job count, machine count and remaining input parameter. The complete instance is supplied before scheduling begins. No unproved complexity assumption is included in this existence question.
cards.definitions:
Instance. There are jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\), positive integer processing times \(p_j\), a positive integer machine count \(m\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,F)\). An arc \((i,j)\in F\) requires job \(i\) to finish before job \(j\) starts. Every arc is a requirement; its transitive consequences also hold. There is no promise on the shape or depth of the directed acyclic graph, and the machine count is not fixed in advance. Every job may run on every machine, and every machine takes exactly \(p_j\) units of time to process job \(j\).

Schedule and feasibility. A schedule specifies for each job a machine \(a_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a nonnegative start time \(s_j\). The job occupies precisely the half-open interval \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\) on that machine. Intervals on the same machine must be pairwise disjoint, and
\[s_j\ge s_i+p_i\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in F.\]
Execution is continuous and uninterrupted: no job may be split, preempted or migrated. Finishing one job and starting another at the same instant is allowed. All jobs are available initially subject to their precedences. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup times, machine eligibility restrictions or other resource constraints. The schedule uses the same number of unit-speed machines as the optimum; extra machines or speed are not allowed.

Objective. The makespan is the latest completion time,
\[C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j\in J}(s_j+p_j),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{S\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(S).\]
This is elapsed time from zero, not the sum or average of completion times. The optimum is positive and at most \(W=\sum_j p_j\). It is unchanged if start times are restricted to nonnegative integers: for any feasible schedule, retain its machine assignments and within-machine job orders and start each job as early as those orders and the precedences allow. Positive integer durations give an acyclic augmented order and integral earliest starts without increasing the makespan. Thus an optimal integer schedule exists. Having more than \(n\) machines offers no advantage, although the full encoded value of \(m\) is counted in the input length.

Encoding. For an integer \(i\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(i+1\) and set \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), with exactly \(\ell\) bits in the last part. Encode an instance as \(U(n)U(m)U(p_1)\cdots U(p_n)\) followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits of \(D\) in row-major order. Valid inputs have the stated positivity and acyclicity properties. Encode an output schedule as the list \(U(a_1)U(s_1)\cdots U(a_n)U(s_n)\), with integer starts. These are explicit binary data, not succinct circuits or value oracles. All output bits and arithmetic costs count.

Algorithms and improvement. Computation uses a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet, no advice, oracle or random bits. Polynomial time is in the full input bit length, including durations and machine count. All computation and output costs count. Invalid encodings may be rejected. The same algorithm, positive \(\varepsilon\) and polynomial constants must work for every valid input; \(\varepsilon\) is not an input accuracy parameter. In particular, the improvement cannot shrink as the number of machines or jobs grows.

For background notation, let \(\mathcal R\subseteq[1,\infty)\) be the universal approximation factors achievable by uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithms for this model, and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=\inf\mathcal R\). context_blocks.text: The input is an entire task graph, not a stream of arrivals. A scheduler may inspect all durations and dependencies before choosing assignments and start times. It must place every job, keep each job uninterrupted, and minimize the last completion time. Changing to an online rule, preemption, machine-dependent durations or total completion time changes the problem.

Total work \(W=\sum_j p_j\) gives the lower bound \(W/m\) on any feasible makespan. The total duration \(D\) of a longest directed path in the precedence graph gives another lower bound, since that chain runs sequentially. The difficulty is that filling machines now and finishing jobs that unlock future work can call for different priorities.

Graham’s list scheduling starts available jobs according to a priority order when machines become free. A job is available after all its predecessors finish. The established bound is \(C_{\max}\le W/m+(1-1/m)D\le(2-1/m)\operatorname{OPT}\). Although this is below two for each finite \(m\), its supremum over input machine counts is two. It therefore gives the universal bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\), not a fixed improvement below two.

A priority example separates a poor list from algorithmic impossibility. For \(m\ge2\), take \(m(m-1)\) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length \(m\). Listing the long job last gives makespan \(2m-1\), whereas starting it immediately and distributing the units over the other machines gives makespan \(m\), which also equals the work lower bound. This shows tightness for that list order; it has no precedence edges and does not prove hardness for every algorithm.

Classical NP-hardness excludes every factor strictly below \(4/3\) unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Consequently \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) implies \(4/3\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The word “unless” is essential: NP-hardness is not an unconditional proof that a polynomial-time algorithm cannot exist.

If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), feasible integer schedules of polynomial bit length can be found optimally in polynomial time, so \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=1\). Here all optimum starts lie at most at total processing time, whose binary length is polynomial in the input length. Thus an unconditional lower bound strictly above one would in particular separate P from NP. Thus conditional hardness must remain distinguished from an unconditional negative answer to the algorithm-existence question.

Svensson proves a transfer from the approximability of a different objective: total weighted completion time on a single machine with precedences. Hardness arbitrarily close to two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit jobs. The transferred loss tends to zero, but the two scheduling objectives and their approximation parameters are not identical.

His Corollary 1 uses the Bansal–Khot Unique Games variant in Appendix Hypothesis 1. It requires a satisfiable large bipartite portion in the completeness case and an extra expansion condition in the soundness case. The difficulty is that filling machines now and finishing jobs that unlock future work can call for different priorities.
